In [[probability]] and business [[statistics]], the '''Bates distribution''', named after [[Grace Bates]], is a [[probability distribution]] of the [[mean]] of a number of [[statistically independent]]  [[continuous uniform distribution|uniformly distributed]] [[random variable]]s on the [[unit interval]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=Norman L. |last2=Kotz |first2=Samuel |last3=Balakrishnan |first3=Narayanaswamy |chapter=Related Distributions |pages=296–306 |chapter-url={{GBurl|BTANEAAAQBAJ|p=296}} |title=Continuous Univariate Distributions, Volume 2 |date=1995 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-58494-0 }}</ref> This distribution is related to the [[Continuous uniform distribution|uniform]], the [[Triangular distribution|triangular]], and the [[Normal distributions|normal Gaussian distribution]], and has applications in [[broadcast engineering]] for signal enhancement. 

The Bates distribution on <math>[0,1]</math> and of parameter <math>n</math> is sometimes confused<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://github.com/d3/d3/issues/1647|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201212211649/https://github.com/d3/d3/issues/1647|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 12, 2020|title=The thing named "Irwin-Hall distribution" in d3.random is actually a Bates distribution · Issue #1647 · d3/d3|website=GitHub|language=en|access-date=2018-04-17}}</ref> with the [[Irwin–Hall distribution]] of parameter <math>n</math>, which is the distribution of the '''sum''' (not the '''mean''') of <math>n</math> independent random variables uniformly distributed on the unit interval <math>[0,1]</math>. More precisely, if <math>X</math> has a Bates distribution on <math>[0,1]</math>, then <math>nX</math> has an [[Irwin–Hall distribution|Irwin-Hall distribution]] of parameter <math>n</math> (and support on <math>[0,n]</math>). For <math>n=1</math>, both the Bates distribution and the Irwin-Hall distribution coincide  with the uniform distribution on the unit interval <math>[0,1]</math>.

==Definition==
The Bates distribution on the [[unit interval]] <math>[0,1]</math> and with parameter <math>n \in \mathbb N</math> is the continuous [[probability distribution]] of the [[empirical mean]] <math>X</math> of <math>n</math> [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[random variable]]s <math>U_1,...,U_n</math> [[continuous uniform distribution|uniformly distributed]] on the [[unit interval]]:

:<math>
X = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n U_k.
</math>

The [[probability density function]] is

: <math>f_X(x; n)= \frac n {2(n-1)!} \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k {n \choose k} (nx-k)^{n-1} \sgn(nx-k)</math><ref>Arnholt AT, Bauldry WC, Rupasinghe HS, Don A, Watagoda LC. Examining the “n≥ 30 is Sufficiently Large for the Sampling Distribution of X to Follow a Normal Distribution” Caveat. BEIO. 2018 Nov:182. https://www.seio.es/beio/BEIOVol34Num3.pdf#page=13</ref>

for <math>
x 
</math> in the open interval <math>
]0,1[ 
</math>, and zero elsewhere. Here <math>\sgn(nx-k)</math> denotes the [[sign function]]:

:<math> \sgn(nx-k) = \begin{cases} 
-1 &  nx < k \\
0 &  nx = k \\
1 &  nx > k. \end{cases}
</math>

More generally, the empirical mean <math>
X^{(a,b)} 
</math> of <math>
n 
</math> [[independence (probability theory)|independent]] random variables <math>
U_1^{(a,b)},...,U_n^{(a,b)} 
</math> [[continuous uniform distribution|uniformly distributed]]  on the interval <math>
[a,b] 
</math>

:<math>
X^{(a,b)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n U_k^{(a,b)}
</math>

has the following the probability density function (PDF) of

:<math> f_{X^{(a,b)}} (x; n) = \frac{1}{b-a} f_X\left(\frac{x-a}{b-a};n\right) </math>
for <math>
x \in ]a,b[
</math> and zero otherwise.

==Extensions and Applications==
{{expand section|date=February 2020}}
With a few modifications, the Bates distribution encompasses the [[Continuous uniform distribution|uniform]], the [[Triangular distribution|triangular]], and, taking the limit as n goes to infinity, also the [[Normal distribution|normal Gaussian distribution]].{{fact|date=May 2025}}

Replacing the term <math> \frac{1}{n} </math> when calculating the mean, ''X'', with <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}</math> will create a similar distribution with a constant variance, such as unity. Then, by subtracting the mean, the resulting mean of the distribution will be set at zero. Thus the parameter ''n'' would become a purely [[Shape parameter|shape-adjusting parameter]]. By also allowing ''n'' to be a non-integer, a highly flexible distribution can be created, for example, ''U''(0,1) + 0.5''U''(0,1) gives a [[trapezoidal distribution]].{{fact|date=May 2025}}

The [[Student-t distribution]] provides a natural extension of the normal Gaussian distribution for modeling of [[long tail]] data. A Bates distribution that has been generalized as previously stated fulfills the same purpose for [[Short-tailed distribution|short tail]] data.{{fact|date=May 2025}}

The Bates distribution has an application to [[beamforming]] and [[pattern synthesis]] in the field of [[electrical engineering]]. The distribution was found to increase the [[beamwidth]] of the [[main lobe]], representing an increase in the signal of the radiation pattern in a single direction, while simultaneously reducing the usually undesirable<ref>{{cite conference |first1=Kristopher |last1=Buchanan |first2=Timi |last2=Adeyemi |first3=Carlos |last3=Flores-Molina |first4=Sara |last4=Wheeland |first5=Drew |last5=Overturf |title=Sidelobe behavior and bandwidth characteristics of distributed antenna arrays |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8299700 |conference=2018 United States National Committee of URSI National Radio Science Meeting (USNC-URSI NRSM) |location=Boulder, CO |date=January 2018 |pages=1–2 |isbn=978-1-946815-02-6 }}</ref> [[Side lobe|sidelobe]] levels.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B0-12-227410-5/00445-2 |chapter=Microwave Communications |title=Encyclopedia of Physical Science and Technology |date=2003 |last1=Berger |first1=U.S. |pages=777–798 |isbn=978-0-12-227410-7 }}</ref>
